name: Ecdysterone

lead: Ecdysterone (20-hydroxyecdysone) is the molting hormone of insects and crustaceans, also found in plants such as spinach and Cyanotis. Lifters take it as a plant-derived anabolic, with some promoting it as a hormone-neutral way to add muscle and a bigger physique.

In rodents it stimulates muscle protein synthesis without androgen receptor activity, with evidence pointing to estrogen receptor beta and Akt signalling. A 2019 controlled study funded by the World Anti-Doping Agency reported larger gains in muscle mass and bench press with ecdysterone alongside training, while a 2006 study found no significant effect on training adaptations. Replication is sparse.

paras: Sold as capsules or powder and taken daily alongside a normal training and protein routine over several weeks. It is also being developed as an investigational compound for muscle conditions.
Acute toxicity appears low. It is sold as a supplement, though the World Anti-Doping Agency has monitored it. Product purity is reported to vary, and long-term human safety has not been established.

angle.text: Lifters take ecdysterone as a plant-derived anabolic to add muscle on top of training, some describing it as hormone-neutral. One controlled human study reported larger gains in muscle mass and bench press with it, and cell and animal work points to estrogen receptor beta. Product quality is a recurring concern.

lead: Ecdysterone, more formally 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E), is a naturally occurring ecdysteroid hormone that controls molting and metamorphosis in insects and crustaceans; it is also produced by plants such as Cyanotis vaga, Ajuga turkestanica and Rhaponticum carthamoides, where it is thought to defend against herbivores [1]. Spinach and quinoa are listed among dietary sources [2].

Mammals lack the arthropod ecdysone receptor, but ecdysterone still affects mammalian systems, and in mammals it is hypothesised to bind estrogen receptor beta (ERbeta) [1][3]. It is sold as a supplement for bodybuilding and sport and is also being developed as an investigational compound for muscle-related conditions [1][4].

Research on its anabolic effects in people is limited. A 2006 study concluded that a modest oral amount did not significantly affect training adaptations, while a 2019 controlled study funded by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) reported larger increases in muscle mass and bench press performance with ecdysterone than without [1][5]. Replication evidence is sparse.
infobox: Insects and crustaceans; Cyanotis vaga, Ajuga turkestanica, Rhaponticum carthamoides, spinach [1][2]

paras: Ecdysterone is marketed in bodybuilding supplements. T Nation members describe adding it to pre-workouts and stacks alongside ashwagandha, tongkat ali, fadogia, laxogenin and turkesterone [6][7][8][9], and some report that it made a 'noteworthy difference' in strength, recovery, body fat and well-being in combination with other products [6]. A 2021 poster recommends only 'proper products with standardized contents' [10]. Another suggests it as a way to lower estrogen effects instead of raising testosterone, warning of underdosed supplements [11].

In 2001 a T Nation thread proposed a forum experiment to test ecdysterone, asking supporters to supply numbers [12]. In 2007 a user described smoking a suma root powder containing 2 percent ecdysterone as an experiment [13].

Registered trials include 20E in sarcopenia (NCT03452488), in prediabetes (NCT03906201), in giardiasis (NCT04827537), and in patients with obesity starting semaglutide to assess muscle wasting (NCT07411378) [14][15][16][17]. Wikipedia notes the FDA approved a study of 20E in obesity in 2024 [1].

A 2006 study found that 30 mg per day orally did not significantly change anabolic or catabolic responses, body composition or training adaptations [1]. A 2019 controlled clinical trial in Archives of Toxicology, funded by WADA, reported significantly greater increases in muscle mass and one-repetition bench press in participants given ecdysterone, with a dose-responsive effect [1][5]. A 2025 12-week randomised double-blind training study tested a commercial phytosteroid product containing 20E and diosgenin and examined the reliability of its labelling [18]. A 2024 review covers ecdysterone and turkesterone in sport [2].

Grokipedia summarises human trials as mixed and attributes some null results to commercial supplements containing far less 20E than labelled [19]; this is from an AI-generated source and was not independently verified.

Long-term human safety has not been established in the sources cited. Grokipedia describes animal data as showing low toxicity [19]. Forum users caution about underdosed supplements and recommend standardised products [10][11].

In arthropods 20E acts through the ecdysone receptor [1]. In mammals, a 2014 study reported that estrogen receptor beta is involved in skeletal muscle hypertrophy induced by ecdysterone [3], and the WADA-funded human study's abstract states that the anabolic effect is thought to be mediated by estrogen receptor binding [5]. Wikipedia describes relatively selective activation of ERbeta in human muscle cells [1]. Grokipedia adds activation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathways [19].
Research on other effects includes bone regeneration via BMP-2/SMAD/RUNX2 signalling and protection of rat liver mitochondria under immobilisation stress, both preclinical [20][21].

Wikipedia notes high oral bioavailability in animals [1]. Studies have examined urinary excretion of ecdysterone and its metabolites after spinach consumption and possible dietary sources of ecdysterone in urine, relevant to anti-doping interpretation [22][23].

Ecdysteroid research began with insect hormones; Grokipedia states 20E was first isolated from the silk moth in the 1960s [19]. Studies in Drosophila in the 1970s and 1980s used ecdysterone to study gene induction and heat-shock responses [24]. Wikipedia describes use of ecdysteroids as inducers in transgenic animals as a research tool [1]. In supplement culture, a 2001 T Nation thread already debated whether ecdysterone 'works' [12].

Human trials of ecdysterone for muscle: a 2006 study [1], the 2019 WADA-funded study [5], and the 2025 12-week trial of a 20E and diosgenin product [18]. Reviews: ecdysterone and turkesterone in sport and nutrition [2] and degenerative diseases [25].
Registered trials listed above cover sarcopenia, prediabetes, giardiasis and obesity with semaglutide [14][15][16][17].

lore.intro: On T Nation ecdysterone has been a subject of debate since the early 2000s and is now typically mentioned as an add-on supplement, with repeated cautions about product quality [12][10][11].
